posts.hook: We already pay for the water we don't use.
posts.body:
The Water Reuse Outlook 2026 looked at 14 countries:
• only 2.4% of treated municipal wastewater was reused in 2025;
• at the same time, 61% of utilities reported at least one drought-related supply restriction in the past five years.

More than 97% of water that has already been collected, treated and paid for goes back to the river, while utilities ration supply.

Scarcity is not only a supply problem. It is an allocation problem.

This is close to how we think at AquaRE: before looking for a new source, look at the water balance you already have.
posts.closing_question: Which utility will be the first to treat its effluent as a product, not a by-product?
posts.source_line: Source: Water Reuse Outlook 2026, Example Water Institute

posts.hook: What does a cubic metre of new water actually cost?
posts.body:
When a region runs short, the default answer is often desalination. The numbers suggest asking a different question first.

According to the Water Reuse Outlook 2026:
• the median cost of water fit for irrigation reuse was €0.38 per cubic metre;
• seawater desalination came in at €0.92 per cubic metre;
• plants with anaerobic digestion and CHP covered on average 47% of their own electricity demand.

Reuse is not the cheap option. It is the economic option.

Before the next large supply investment, the question should be: how much of the demand could the effluent we already treat cover?
posts.source_line: Source: Water Reuse Outlook 2026, Example Water Institute

posts.hook: Technology alone is not enough. The operators say so too.
posts.body:
I often hear that water reuse is waiting for better technology. The utility managers in the Water Reuse Outlook 2026 see it differently:
• 72% named permitting and unclear quality rules as the biggest barrier;
• financing came second at 41%;
• public acceptance, the one we worry about most, was 23%.

The treatment works. What is missing is a clear answer to who sets the quality standard and who signs off.

Regulation is infrastructure too.

And if we measure the cost of inaction, we should also ask: how much water have unclear rules already cost us?
posts.closing_question: Which rule would you rewrite first?
posts.source_line: Source: Water Reuse Outlook 2026, Example Water Institute

article.title: The cheapest new water is already flowing out of our treatment plants
article.subtitle: Three figures from the Water Reuse Outlook 2026, and why water risk is economic risk
article.body_markdown:
Managing water scarcity begins long before water scarcity. It begins with knowing what water we already have, and what we do with it.

## We treat it, then we let it go

The Water Reuse Outlook 2026 surveyed 14 countries. Only 2.4% of treated municipal wastewater was reused in 2025. The collection network, the treatment, the energy and the people running the plant have all been paid for. The water leaving the plant has value. It simply has no buyer yet.

At the same time, 61% of utilities reported at least one drought-related supply restriction in the past five years. Scarcity is already part of normal operations, not a future scenario.

## The economic case

The usual objection to reuse is cost. The data points the other way. The median cost of producing water fit for irrigation reuse was €0.38 per cubic metre, compared with €0.92 per cubic metre for seawater desalination.

This matters most where the pressure is highest: regions with farming inland and a desalination plant on the table as the default answer.

## The size of the opportunity

If every country in the survey reached the reuse share already achieved by the leading country, an additional 1.1 billion cubic metres of water per year would be available for agriculture and industry.

This is not a technology forecast. It is what happens if the others catch up with someone who has already done it.

## Technology alone is not enough

The barrier is mostly regulation and organisation: who defines the quality class, who carries the risk, who signs off. That is where the work is, and where cooperation between utilities, regulators and water users decides the outcome.

Water risk is economic risk. The question is not whether we can afford to reuse water, but how long we can afford not to.

Source: Water Reuse Outlook 2026, Example Water Institute (sample report).
